title: Firefox Can Now Block Ads on iOS (but You Have to Enable It)
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 1, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Kenneth Cheung / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device, as Mozilla is officially rolling out native ad blocking.
                                            Most ads will be blocked, but users will still see search engine ads and sponsored content from Firefox.
                                            The feature is off by default, so you need to enable it yourself if you want to use it.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device. Following a slow "experimental" period, Mozilla is now officially rolling out native ad blocking, which you can enable once the tool is available in your app. According to Mozilla's support page detailing the new feature, Firefox's new feature can block third-party ad networks and exchanges along with many third-party ads served on websites at the network level. It can also block ad-related trackers, pop-ups, and overlays. The platform is still letting some ads through, though: For example, you'll still see ads in search results from engines like Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo, as well as sponsored content on the Firefox Home and New Tab pages. There may also be ads that aren't covered by the EasyList filter list. Of course, Firefox isn't the only browser to natively block ads on iOS. For example, both DuckDuckGo and Brave have built-in ad blocking in their mobile apps and also allow you to disable their own search ads. Note that ad-blocking functionality doesn't extend outside of the Firefox iOS app, but URL filters in iOS 26, along with a third-party app like Wipr 2, can block ads in other apps. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Ad blocking in Firefox will be off by default. To enable it, open the iOS app, tap the three dots, and go to Settings > Browsing. Under the Content header, toggle on Ad Blocker. You can do this from the Site menu by tapping Ad Blocker (underneath the site name and URL), which will open the Browsing menu directly. The site menu will show you at a glance whether ad blocking is on or off.

            Credit: Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft Outlook is down for many users as of Monday afternoon.
                                            Downdetector highlights tens of thousands of users reports suggesting issues with Outlook.
                                            In addition, other Microsoft services, including Microsoft 365, are also down.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're trying to check your inbox or send an email in Microsoft Outlook, only to find the app uncooperative, you're not alone. Outlook is currently down for many users as of Monday afternoon. That's apparent to anyone who can't get the app to work: Downdetector, which highlights user reports for app outages, shows tens of thousands of reports as of 3:00 p.m. ET, and while the rate of reports does seem to be decreasing, thousands of reports keep coming in with every refresh.  As CNET reports, Microsoft has officially confirmed the outage itself. The company posted on its Microsoft 365 Status X account, stating: “We’ve identified an issue with an authentication component which is contributing to impact. To address this, we’ve developed a remediation strategy, and we’re applying it to a portion of infrastructure to test its efficacy. Once we’ve confirmed this resolves impact, we’ll apply the solution more broadly. For more information, please see EX1464935 in the admin center.”As such, the company should be rolling out a fix in due time, though it's difficult to say how long that may be. Recent outages have been fixed in a matter of hours, while others have stretched into the following day. At the time of writing, Downdetector shows that 38% of users are reporting issues receiving messages in Outlook, while 24% report issues with the app, and 21% with logging in. 
As it happens, Outlook isn't the only Microsoft product facing issues: Users report that Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Store, Microsoft Azur  and Microsoft 365 in general are experiencing  issues. In addition, OpenAI users are reporting issues with ChatGPT. 
            
                What do you think so far?

title: What Is This 'Android Pulse' App Appearing on Everybody's Phones?
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: georgeclerk via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Android users started seeing a new "Android Pulse" app on their phones over the weekend. As it turns out, it's supposed to be there.
                                            Android Pulse is a Google-made app that works in the background to note any apps or processes that take up too many resources on your phone.
                                            The Play Store says the app is three days old, with over 10 million downloads, though APKMirror shows that Android Pulse has existed since March.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you keep tabs on your Android app updates in the Play Store, you might have noticed something odd: You have an app called "Android Pulse" on your phone. Most of us have way too many apps on our phones, and it's easy to forget that we downloaded some of them—especially when we install them once and never use them again. But I'd wager that not only do you have no recollection of downloading Android Pulse, but you have no idea what Android Pulse even is. I had certainly never heard of Android Pulse before Monday morning, though I admit I spend far more time on iOS than on Android. Luckily, I don't think any level of Android knowledge or use would prime one to know about the app, as it appears Android Pulse is only three days old. As reported by 9to5Google, Android Pulse started appearing in Play Store updates as early as Saturday morning. In fact, its Play Store listing shows that it was released on August 21 of this year by none other than Google itself. And yet, after only three days on the Play Store, Android Pulse has over 10 million downloads.    Android Pulse has been working in the background on your phoneAs it turns out, Google didn't silently install a random app on tens of millions of Android users' devices. Rather, it's the Play Store listing itself that's new, not Android Pulse. According to its Play Store description, Android Pulse "facilitates rule distribution for anomaly detection in critical system resource consumption by the Android operating system and installed applications." 
In layman's terms? Android Pulse keeps a virtual eye out for any suspicious processes that consume excessive system resources in both Android and your phone's apps. There are many possibilities there: It may be that Android Pulse looks for apps that put an unnecessary strain on the CPU or GPU, or system processes that drain your battery more than usual. Whatever the case, Android Pulse monitors for unusual activity affecting your phone and how it functions. And despite its new "app," there isn't much you can do with it. It isn't even clear if Android Pulse helps Android OS fix itself, or if Google simply receives the reports to help with future stability updates.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Interestingly, while the Play Store says the app is three days old, APKMirror says its first iteration dropped in March. Whatever the case, Android Pulse only made itself known this weekend, so it's news to most—if not all—of us. What should I do about Android Pulse?The short answer? Nothing. Android Pulse appears to be a background system resource that just so happens to appear in app form. In fact, based on screenshots from Android Authority, it doesn't even appear that you can uninstall it. You might be able to disable or force stop Pulse, but I'm not sure you'd want to. The "app" is designed to root out system hogs; I suspect it won't become one itself.

title: This Is the Best Ad-Free Alternative to Apple Maps
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 26, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Prykhodov via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple Maps officially launched ads in search this week.
                                            You'll see ads in the new "Suggested Places" field, as well as in Apple Maps search results.
                                            You can't block Apple Maps ads, but you can choose an alternative that skips out on them completely.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        This week, Apple Maps officially launched ads in search. It's not necessarily a surprise, mind you: We learned back in October that Apple planned to roll out ads at some point. But it's still a bit jarring to see Apple actually commit to the plan. Now, most of the mainstream navigation apps come with ads, which makes getting around without dealing with ads difficult—but not impossible.How Apple Maps' ads work Once ads hit your app, you'll start seeing them when you search for new destinations. That includes both in the new "Suggested Places" section, as well as within search results as well. Like other platforms that float sponsored items to the top of search results, you'll likely want to be a bit more scrupulous, since the top pick might not actually be the most relevant to your query. What's more, there's no way to actually disable these ads. There are ad blockers for iPhone, but they're limited, and won't block Apple's own ads. As such, it just doesn't feel very "Apple" to deal with ads on the company's own navigation app—especially if you're already giving Apple money every month. While Apple Maps doesn't have a paid subscription, Apple offers plenty of services at a cost. As YouTuber Quinn Nelson notes, some users are paying $50 per month for Apple One, and still having to deal with ads on Apple Maps. Of course, it's the same story for Google Maps: Google's famous navigation app also has mandatory ads, whether you subscribe to one of Google's services or not. In Apple's view, its approach is better than competitors like Google, as the company is adamant its ads preserve your privacy. But even if that's the case, I'm not sure it's going to sell users on the new approach.
It's tough to find a good navigation alternative to Apple Maps or Google Maps. That includes Waze, which is also owned by Google and also has ads. However, there is one solid—albeit rather underground—choice for anyone whose top priority is a lack of ads.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Organic Maps is a free and open-source app that prioritizes privacy for navigation. According to the developer, the app works entirely offline, and does not track people as they use it. (How refreshing.) As such, you could download your maps, disable cellular services, and still have the ability to navigate—of course, you can use it while connected, as well. The app supports a number of features that you'll find on other more mainstream platforms, including cycling and hiking routes, turn-by-turn directions, public transit maps, and dark mode. Organic Maps uses OpenStreetMap to provide its navigation data. While the benefit of OpenStreetMap is that it's also open-source, so users all over the globe can add their own data points, it likely isn't as robust as Apple's map data, not to mention Google's decades of data. Still, users have generally positive reviews on the iOS App Store, suggesting that OpenStreetMap's data offers an adequate alternative to Apple Maps. Now, if you're used to scrolling through restaurant reviews or checking out Street View, you'll miss that here. While Organic Maps does have a search function, it's lacking compared to other platforms. This is definitely a navigation-first app, rather than a full Apple Maps or Google Maps replacement. Still, if you're looking for an ad-free alternative, there are few better options out there at this time.

title: RayNeo Is Launching Two New Lines of Smart Glasses
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: RayNeo
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            RayNeo announced the RayNeo iO and the RayNeo GT Series.
                                            The iO features a monochrome display; the GT features high-def video.
                                            Both product lines release on September 4, 2026.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Smart glass company RayNeo announced two new lines of smart glasses today: the minimal-display, AI-focused RayNeo iO, and the RayNeo GT and the GT Max, which are portable monitor glasses. They will all be available on Sept. 4 through RayNeo's site and on Amazon, but no prices were announced.The company is aiming at two distinct segments of the smart glasses market with these models. The IO is productivity-minded, with a minimal monocular display, audio capability, and AI integration, where the GT series are tethered display glasses mainly for entertainment. What to know about RayNeo's IO productivity glassesRayNeo's IO glasses are a definite change for the company. Its last display glasses, RayNeo X3 Pros, are built around a full-color, high-definition display. I found them technically impressive, but not especially practical. These new glasses, though, seem like they will be a lot more useful. Here's what they bring to the table:
Lightweight frame designed for comfort. These glasses weigh only 33 grams, as light as an average pair of non-display glasses. A minimal, monochrome waveguide display that's only visible to the wearer. Integrated Ambient AI. Powered by Gemini's AI, RayNeo says their "Life Log" operates in the background and can "capture schedules and conversation contexts." It will extract action items and schedule calendar updates after meetings too. Translation and teleprompter features: There's no audio, so translations and audio are all handled in the display. Long battery life: The company promises two days of typical usage per charge.Overall, the IO glasses sound a lot like Even Realities' excellent G2 smart glasses. The main negative for these and any glasses with a waveguide display is that the lenses have to be totally flat, so they're generally small, or else they look very strange. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What to know about the RayNeo's GT SeriesThe GT series from RayNeo are designed to stream content and provide a second monitor, as opposed to being worn all day. They are basically an improved version of RayNeo's "wearable monitor" style glasses like the RayNeo Air 4. Here's what the GT series bring to the table:59° field of view. This is a big improvement over the 47° FOV of the Air 4 and puts it in the same league as the industry-leading display glasses, XReal's One Pro. Peacock optical engine 3.0 Max and a 5.5th-gen tandem MicroOLED display that's the equivalent of a 307" monitor. Dolby Vision support: Paired with the RayNeo Pocket TV Pro, the GT Series supports native Dolby Vision playback alongside real-time AI SDR-to-HDR conversion.Bang & Olufsen spatial audio: A quad-speaker system supports head-tracked spatial audio and directional sound transmission.The GT Max comes in three physical Interpupillary Distance (IPD) sizes for better clarity across different face shapes and sizes. Maybe the most notable thing about these glasses is what they lack: Neither has a camera, even though RayNeo's last generation of display-style glasses did. Huge tech companies like Meta and Snap have bet bigs on people wanting face-cameras, but with the IO, RayNeo seems to be taking the stance that discretion and a low-key utility are a stronger position.

title: I Gave ChatGPT Access to My iMessage Conversations, and It Was More Useful Than I Expected
body:
David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Lifehacker
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Installing the ChatGPT desktop app gives you a few extras that aren't available through the web portal, including the ability to run prompts that query your local files, emails, and screenshots. Now, with the macOS client, those additional features extend to your iMessages, too: There's now an Apple Messages plug-in available.The idea of giving ChatGPT access to your chats is something a lot of users aren't ever going to countenance—"good luck with that spy software" is one typical response on Reddit—but we know that plenty of users are already asking AI for help in composing and interpreting messages. This just makes that process more streamlined. (Claude has an Apple Messages plug-in too, for what it's worth.)As OpenAI confirmed to TechCrunch, the plug-in does all its processing on your Mac, and doesn't send anything about your chats back to servers in the cloud—these Messages conversations won't appear in your ChatGPT apps on the web or on mobile. In addition, the ChatGPT desktop app doesn't build a full index of your text messages.
This is something that's available for all ChatGPT users who have a Mac: To get started, download and install the desktop app for macOS, then open the Plugins tab, search for "messages," and click Install next to the Apple Messages entry. You can then use natural language in your prompts to invoke the plug-in ("send a message to..."), use the @Messages mention, or select Messages from the plug-in list in the prompt box (click the + icon to find it).
    
            
            You'll need to give the plug-in specific permission to operate.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Once you've set it up, ChatGPT can then do just about anything you can imagine with your messages, starting with the basics: It'll send messages for you, for example, and even compose them if you're stuck for inspiration. You just have to name the contact, so something like "message Steve telling him I'm sorry I can't come to his dinner party in a polite way" will do exactly that.When I tried this, ChatGPT whipped up a suitably friendly message, with the right blend of thank yous, sorrys, and hopes for a lovely evening. When sending messages, you get the option to review what's being sent and approve it before it goes out—you can approve messages each time, or have them sent automatically in the conversations you select.Then there's everything the AI is able to do with your message history. You can use prompts like "who's messaged me the most this week?" or "is there anything I need to follow up on in my conversations?" and have ChatGPT take a look.I tried getting ChatGPT to dig back into my message history for details of event arrangements and deliveries, and it picked out the right information each time. I also got it to look back over text messages from my phone carrier to see if my bill had gone up over time, which it had: The AI gave me the exact increase, and the percentage increase, together with the relevant dates.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        

    
            
            ChatGPT can send messages to your contacts, with your approval.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Conversations can continue based on whatever you find as well, so if you discover there's a chat thread with an invite that you haven't responded to, ChatGPT can sort that for you—and may even draft a suitable reply you can approve with a couple of clicks, depending on the context.It's in this message history retrieval and analysis where the ChatGPT plug-in seems most useful to me. I'm reluctant to start farming out message composing and sending duties to AI—it seems rude, first and foremost, not to mention bad for my brain—but searching through reams of text is something that AI does well, and could genuinely end up saving me some time.If you're prepared to trust ChatGPT with access to your Apple Messages chat list (and that's a big "if") then it's another database for the AI to mine and analyze. As with a lot of these other plug-ins, like Claude and Gmail, it's a question of where you're going to draw the line between privacy and convenience.And there are certainly risks to watch out for: I can see this being yet another way that people become over-reliant on AI and its "thoughts." If you want ChatGPT to assess someone's mood over time based on their chat history, or compose a message that gives you the best chance of rekindling a relationship, or write a text getting you out of work based on a fake excuse that sounds genuine, ChatGPT will do it. That's where the tech veers beyond the useful and straight into the uncomfortable.

schema.headline: I Gave ChatGPT Access to My iMessage Conversations, and It Was More Useful Than I Expected

title: Why You Might Need to Roll Back Windows' Latest Update
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 31, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NguyenDucQuang via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft's latest Windows update comes with cool new features that users have been asking for. Unfortunately, it comes with glaring bugs as well.
                                            The update makes it possible to move and resize the task bar, and introduces improvements to Windows Search.
                                            At the same time, it breaks the cursor, hiding it entirely or making it too small or large. In addition, your wallpaper may disappear, and fonts may be blurry.
                                            The only workaround at this time is uninstalling the latest update, which luckily isn't difficult or dangerous to do.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're the kind of person who installs Windows updates as soon as they hit your PC, you're likely running version KB5120998 of Windows 11 right now. Microsoft released it on Thursday, and while it's an optional update, it isn't locked behind its Windows Insider program. As such, anyone who has manually checked for new updates since then will have seen it, and could have installed it. Unfortunately, that might have been a mistake.  As reported by Windows Insider, the latest Windows 11 update is a big one. It includes some major updates to Windows customization, including changes that Microsoft has been testing for months. For example, the update lets you move and resize the taskbar however you like, and there are other changes that improve Windows Search for the better. These updates have previouly been exclusive to Insiders, but are now officially part of Windows 11. But it's not all good news.Windows 11's latest update is buggyIn addition to these new features, it seems Microsoft inadvertently shipped some bugs with this update. Perhaps the most impactful of them, and the one most users will notice right away, is an issue where the cursor doesn't appear onscreen—or, when it does, it appears too big or too small. Some users report their cursors are enormous, while others find them annoyingly small. Unless you use your keyboard to control everything on your PC, losing access to your cursor isn't really an option, and even inconsistent UI experiences aren't really acceptable in 2026, considering Windows has had a cursor since 1985.
Luckily, Microsoft has a fix in the works. The company formally addressed the bug on a support page, stating, "Microsoft has received reports indicating that mouse cursor personalization settings are being changed or reverted to certain standard settings. This occurs following installation of Windows updates released August 27 2026 (KB5120998) and later."It's not just the cursor causing issues, though. Following this update, Windows may forget your wallpaper settings, so your desktop appears black. You can bring your wallpaper back, but this glitch may occur every time you restart your PC. There are also reports that some fonts appear blurry, which would be particularly annoying on high-resolution displays. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you're experiencing any or all of these bugs, the only solution at this time appears to be rolling back the update. As Windows Latest highlights, users did see their cursors return to normal following the rollback, and those specific wallpaper glitches were only reported with this latest version. Luckily, it isn't too difficult to uninstall a recent Windows update. To do so, head to Settings > Windows Update > Update History > Uninstall. Here, find the update (KB5120998), then choose "Uninstall." Windows Latest notes that because this update was optional, you won't lose any security patches this way. Hopefully, Windows' next update is a bit more stable than this one.

title: These Google Maps Alternatives Still Call It ‘Lake Ontario’ (for Now)
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 31, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Following Trump's executive order, Google Maps has renamed Lake Ontario to "Lake America."
                                            The company says it follows the U.S. Geographic Names Information System, and has updated its map accordingly.
                                            Some other navigation apps have not changed Lake Ontario's name—at least, not yet.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America." The move was retaliation against Canada for walking away from contentious trade talks and in spite of the fact that Lake Ontario's name has nothing to do with the Canadian province. Regardless, tech companies are now dealing with the consequences.Why did Google Maps change Lake Ontario's name?If you live in the U.S., you may have opened Google Maps this weekend to see that the app had already changed Lake Ontario's name. Even if you don't live in the U.S., you may see the name change: As it happens, there are now three different naming schemes for the lake in Google's navigation app. If you use the app in the U.S., you'll see "Lake America." If you use it in Canada, you'll see "Lake Ontario." If you use it anywhere else in the world, you'll see "Lake Ontario (Lake America)." Thanks, Google.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
Google did the same when Trump "changed" the name of the Gulf of Mexico to "Gulf of America." While Google explains in a blog post that its policy is to follow the naming conventions of the U.S. Geographic Names Information System, it's also arguable that the company doesn't want to get into hot water with the Trump Administration, lest it be punished with future policies that could hurt its trillion-dollar business.  
Whether you consider it basic bureaucratic compliance or corporate cowardice, Google Maps now calls the lake by its "new" name. It doesn't affect how the app works (maybe unless you're looking for directions to, or information about, Lake Ontario), but if the change rankles you, you have other options: As it stands, there are several Google Maps alternatives that still label it "Lake Ontario."As of this writing, most of the navigation apps available to download call Lake Ontario by its official/"former" name. Whether that will remain true as the week goes on remains a question, but for now, the following apps are still reflecting the global consensus:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple MapsMapQuestOrganic MapsTechnically, Waze also still calls it Lake Ontario on its map, and the name pops up when you start to search for it. But once you tap the result, the app then swaps the name to Lake America. That's to be expected, given Google owns Waze, but the app initially tricked me into thinking it had maintained the previous status quo.Will other apps change Lake Ontario's name?Will all these other apps maintain the Lake Ontario name over the long term? Like Google, Apple ultimately changed the Gulf of Mexico's name, so it will likely do the same with the lake. However, MapQuest and Organic Maps still call the Gulf of Mexico by its correct name, so chances are good they'll keep Lake Ontario on their maps for the foreseeable future.
